questions.stem: Mrs Smith, 55, is seen in general practice between attacks of spinning vertigo with right ear symptoms. Otoscopy is normal. You use a 512 Hz tuning fork. Weber's test lateralises to her left ear, and Rinne's test is positive (air conduction louder than bone) on both sides. What do these bedside findings most likely indicate?
questions.why: In a sensorineural loss, Rinne stays positive and Weber lateralises away from the affected ear, towards the better cochlea. So Weber to the left with Rinne positive on both sides means a right sensorineural loss, which fits her audiogram.
notes: A left sensorineural loss would send Weber away from the left ear, to the right.
A right conductive loss would send Weber to the right and make Rinne negative on the right.
A left conductive loss would send Weber to the left, but Rinne would be negative on the left, and here it is positive on both sides.

questions.stem: Mrs Smith, 55, has probable right Ménière's disease. She is reviewed in general practice between attacks while waiting for a non-urgent ENT referral. She asks for something to keep at home for the next attack, since her attacks bring hours of spinning vertigo and repeated vomiting. Which is the most appropriate medicine to prescribe?
options: Prochlorperazine 5 to 10 mg orally up to three times a day, short course only
Betahistine 16 mg orally three times a day, started at the onset of an attack
Diazepam 5 mg orally three times a day, continued between attacks
Prednisolone 50 mg orally daily for 5 days, started at the onset of each attack
questions.why: For acute attacks of Ménière's vertigo with nausea, a short course of a vestibular sedative and antiemetic such as prochlorperazine 5 to 10 mg orally up to three times a day is first-line. Stop it once the attack settles, because long-term use slows central compensation.
notes: Betahistine is sometimes tried for prevention, usually with ENT advice. It has no role in treating an acute attack and the evidence for it is weak.
Regular long-term benzodiazepines slow vestibular compensation and cause dependence and sedation. That is a particular problem for someone who drives and lives alone.
Oral corticosteroids are used for sudden sensorineural hearing loss. They are not a standard treatment for vertigo attacks in general practice.

questions.stem: Mrs Smith, 55, has right Ménière's disease. She has spontaneous 8-hour attacks of vertigo with fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness. The ENT registrar tells her the condition is linked to a disturbance of the fluid in her inner ear. Which best describes the pathological change associated with this disease?
options: Excess perilymph leaking through a fistula at the round window
Calcium carbonate otoconia displaced into the posterior semicircular canal
Inflammation of the superior vestibular nerve after a viral infection
Excess potassium-rich endolymph distending the membranous labyrinth
questions.why: Ménière's disease is associated with endolymphatic hydrops. The stria vascularis secretes potassium-rich endolymph and the endolymphatic sac normally resorbs it. When resorption fails, the cochlear duct and vestibular labyrinth distend, and the low-frequency apex of the cochlea is affected first.
notes: A perilymph fistula usually follows trauma or barotrauma. It causes vertigo set off by pressure or straining, not endolymphatic distension.
Displaced otoconia cause BPPV, which gives positional vertigo lasting seconds and a positive Dix-Hallpike test. Hers was negative.
Vestibular neuritis gives a single episode of continuous vertigo lasting days, without hearing loss and without recurrent discrete attacks.

questions.stem: Mrs Smith, 55, has an asymmetric right sensorineural hearing loss. ENT plans an MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude a vestibular schwannoma. As part of her cranial nerve examination, you test the nerve that runs with the vestibulocochlear nerve through the internal acoustic meatus, because a tumour there can compress it. Which nerve is this?
questions.why: The facial nerve, with its nervus intermedius, runs alongside CN VIII through the internal acoustic meatus. A schwannoma there can cause facial weakness or taste change. Larger tumours that spread into the cerebellopontine angle can also reduce the corneal reflex (CN V).
notes: The trigeminal nerve lies near the cerebellopontine angle and is affected by larger tumours, but it does not pass through the internal acoustic meatus.
The glossopharyngeal nerve leaves the skull through the jugular foramen, not the internal acoustic meatus.
The abducens nerve runs through Dorello's canal and the cavernous sinus to the superior orbital fissure. It does not pass through the internal acoustic meatus.
